title: PLC-Framework project configuration
description: Structural contract for .plc-framework/config.json. It is the only one of the three validators that runs while the file is being typed - Core's run before a save and after a load, and they catch the four rules JSON Schema cannot express: that an implements entry names a rule that exists, that rule ids are unique, that sibling folder names are unique, and that a regex compiles. Draft-07 rather than 2020-12, for editor support; nothing here needs the newer draft.

$schema.description: Points at this file, which is what makes an editor validate while you type.

coreRemoteRepositoryConfig.description: The hosted repository holding the core. Validated only when coreSource is remote; kept but ignored otherwise, as Core ignores it.

coreLocalRepositoryConfig.description: A core on this machine or a mapped drive. Validated only when coreSource is local; kept but ignored otherwise, as Core ignores it.

metadata.description: Holds coreSource, which decides the rest of the file.

coreSource.description: Which repository section this configuration uses, and therefore which one is required. null - or no key at all - means no repository: only the actions that read a core need one. Neither unused section is validated.

version.description: Two to four components of up to two digits each: v2.0, v1.12.3, v9.9.9.9.

remoteRepository.description: The hosted repository holding the core. Required and validated when coreSource is remote, ignored otherwise.

provider.description: Which host's API to speak. Absent means github, which is what every configuration written before this key existed says by omission. It is here rather than in coreSource because that one answers a different question: a folder on this machine, or a repository over a wire.

apiUrl.description: The provider's API endpoint, absolute and http or https: https://api.github.com/ for github.com, or a self-hosted instance's own.

branch.description: Branch to read from. The template ships main.

folder.description: Path inside the repository down to the core.

dependencyFile.description: Dependency graph file name, today core.json.

token.description: Always a ${VARIABLE} reference and never the secret - ${GITHUB_TOKEN} for github: this file lives in a TIA project and TIA projects are under version control, so the value goes to the per-user .env instead. Nothing in the framework knows the variable's name, so a second provider names its own. Absent or empty means a public repository.

localRepository.description: A core on this machine or a mapped drive. Required and validated when coreSource is local, ignored otherwise.

repository.description: Local path to the repository. That it exists is environmental, and checked separately: a configuration is not wrong because a drive is not mapped here.

folder.description: Path inside the repository down to the core.

dependencyFile.description: Dependency graph file name, today core.json.

projectConfig.description: What the Add-In applies to the TIA project.

hierarchy.description: The folder tree to create. Every list is required but may be empty: [] says this concern has no folders, while a missing key says nothing at all.

softwareUnits.description: Applied inside every software unit. Optional as a whole - only the S7-1500 has them, and on an S7-1200 the section is ignored - but once present all three lists are required. There is deliberately no technologyObjects here: a software unit exposes blocks, tag tables and types only.

groupList.description: Folders for one concern. May be empty.

group.description: One folder, and whatever nests inside it.

name.description: Folder name. Must be unique among siblings of the same parent - which JSON Schema cannot check, so Core's validator does. The same name in a different branch is legal: they are different folders.

groups.description: Sub-folders. Same rules, all the way down.

codingStyle.description: Naming rules, and which TIA object types are held to them. Same rule as the hierarchy: every list of type objects is required and may be empty. The rule catalogue is split in two because the two kinds are referenced from different places and never stand in for one another - but their ids are unique across both, so an id in a report names exactly one rule.

objectRules.description: Rules for the names of TIA objects. This is what every implements entry points at, and each may carry an interface saying what belongs inside the object it names.

interfaceRules.description: Rules for the names of what lives inside an object: interface members, tags, constants. Optional, so a configuration written before the catalogue was split stays valid. Referenced only from an object rule's interface.

rules.description: The former name of objectRules, still read so that a configuration already living in a TIA project keeps working. The editor writes the current name, so a document migrates the first time somebody saves it. Carrying both keys is what Core's validator reports.

ruleId.description: Unique across BOTH catalogues - which JSON Schema cannot check, so Core's validator does.

ruleRegex.description: Naming pattern. That it compiles is checked by Core's validator: a pattern that cannot compile is a broken file, not a broken machine. Note an empty pattern would match every name ever written.

ruleDescriptions.description: Human-readable explanation of the rule, one line each.

objectRule.description: One rule for the name of a TIA object.

interfaceRule.description: One rule for the name of something that lives inside an object.

implements.description: The rules held against a name, as ALTERNATIVES: it passes if it matches any one of them. Not empty, and every entry must name an existing rule in the catalogue this list is allowed to reach - object rules from a type, interface rules from an interface. The reference itself is what Core's validator checks, since JSON Schema cannot look across the document.

interfaceSection.description: One section of this type's interface, and the rules its members answer to.

type.description: Closed set, spelled as TIA spells it. The first six are the sections of a block interface; the last two are a tag table's, named apart because a tag and a user constant answer to different rules. Listing the same section twice is what Core's validator catches, since JSON Schema's uniqueItems compares whole objects rather than one field.

interface.description: Optional. Naming rules for what lives inside this object, per interface section. Absent means the interface is not checked - which is the state of every configuration written before this existed. It is nested inside the type rather than declared as a flat variables list because the binding carries the meaning: a static of an FB and a temp of an FC are both variables and may answer to different rules.

type.description: Closed set. A value outside it cannot ever match a real object.
